stubs.how: Local Node HTTP server .ui-capture/stub/server.mjs on 127.0.0.1:4422 serving .ui-capture/stub/db.json (generated by seed.mjs). The app is pointed at it with PUBLIC_LITEKART_API_URL, so SSR calls go there via handleFetch and browser /api/* calls go through the app's own production /api proxy. Carts, wishlist toggles and sessions are kept in memory.

stubs.how: Unsplash sample photos bundled in the @vendure/create npm package, copied to .ui-capture/stub/images and served by the stub at /api/media/<file>; homepage hero/tiles/banner images are set through the store record's theme.content (the Litekart admin override path).

stubs.service: Google Fonts (Inter for the default theme)

stubs.service: Litekart Conversational Shopping assistant (/api/commerce-assistant/*: config, sessions, messages, add-to-cart, events)
stubs.how: Implemented in the stub. /config answers 200 with enabled:false because this store keeps the advisor off (the storefront widget's built-in prompts are jewellery-specific), so the widget stays hidden. Run start.sh with STUB_ASSISTANT=on to enable it; messages are then answered from the catalogue (category + budget parsing, ranked recommendations with prices, ratings, stock and delivery estimates).

app.notes: SvelteKit 2 storefront (Svelte 5) on its stock Litekart connector, run as the production adapter-node build (build/) by .ui-capture/start.sh, which also starts the API stub. Tooling pinned in mise.toml (node 24.22.3, bun 1.4.4); deps via `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, build via `bun run build`. Changes to the repo, all only to make it build/run offline: src/hooks.server.ts reads the optional connector hook setRequestHost via Reflect.get (the production build otherwise turns it into a named import Litekart 2.0.29 does not export and crashes at boot); src/lib/theme/index.ts serves Inter locally; start.sh preloads .ui-capture/node-require-shim.mjs because adapter-node bundles jsdom (used by kitcommerce-core's HTML sanitizer) and its require.resolve breaks under ESM. Data (seed.mjs -> db.json): store 'Northfield Supply Co.' (Oakland, CA, USD) with menus, plugins (wishlist, reviews, coupons, search) and homepage copy; 54 products / 9 categories from Vendure's sample catalog with variants (sizes, RAM/screen, colours), sale prices, sold-out and low-stock items; ~200 reviews; customer Megan Okafor (signed-in account above) with 26 orders over ~16 months (Delivered, Shipped, Processing, Pending, Cancelled, Returned; coupons, COD/PayPal/card), 4 saved addresses, 10 wishlist items, 2 items in her saved bag, 5 of her own reviews; 9 journal posts, 5 policy/about pages, 6 FAQs, 5 coupons. Main areas: home (/), catalogue (/products, category pages like /furniture, /plants, /camera-and-photo), product pages (/products/<slug>), search, cart (/cart, /checkout/*), account (/my, /my/orders, /my/orders/<orderNo e.g. NF-24117>, /my/wishlist, /my/addresses, /my/profile, /my/buy-again), journal (/blog), /faqs, /about-us and policy pages. Sign in from the header account icon with the login above to see the established customer's account, bag and wishlist.

# Running it
- Follow the repo's own setup docs and tooling. Take the simplest route that shows the real app: a static production build if the front end works without a backend, otherwise the app's own server (production or dev mode).
- If it needs a database or other services, run them locally with an embedded or file-based option (SQLite, in-memory, JSON files, an embedded Postgres such as PGlite) or the app's demo/mock mode.
- Don't redesign or restyle anything. Change only what's needed to build and run it.

# Tools: use mise
Install every runtime and tool you need (node, the package manager, python, bun, ...) with mise, pinned to exact versions in a mise.toml at the repo root, so the setup can be reproduced. Match what the repo asks for (engines, .nvmrc, .tool-versions, packageManager). mise is already configured for this directory: `mise install` installs into ./.ui-capture/mise, and its shims come first on PATH, so `node`, `pnpm` and the rest resolve to the pinned versions. Don't use other copies of these tools or download runtimes by hand.

# Secrets, API keys and external services: fake them
The app must not depend on anything outside this machine, and when it runs it has no network except localhost. Wherever it expects secrets, environment variables, API keys or third-party services (hosted auth or OAuth, payment providers, email, LLM or other AI APIs, maps, storage buckets, analytics, hosted databases):
- Give the required variables placeholder values so the app starts.
- Where it actually calls the service, make the call succeed locally with realistic responses: use the app's own mock, test or offline mode if it has one; otherwise point the client at a small local stub server that start.sh also starts, or swap in a stub at the integration boundary (the API client or service module). Keep stubs out of UI code. Responses should look like what the real service returns for a real user, e.g. an AI reply that actually answers, a payment history with real-looking amounts.
- Calls the browser makes directly to outside services count too; point them at the local stub.
- For sign-in through an outside provider, create a local account or use the app's dev sign-in so you can get past it.
List every stub in app.json.

# Data: like real use
Seed it the way an established user's data would look after months of actual use: specific, plausible names and content for this kind of app; dates spread over time; a realistic mix of states (done, in progress, overdue, archived, ...); realistic volume (dozens to hundreds of records where the app revolves around records); short and long text; some messiness real data has. Start from the app's own demo or seed data if it has realistic data, and extend it if it's thin. Load data through the app's own paths (its API, import, seed scripts, or its database schema), never by hardcoding it into UI code. If the app needs an account, create one and attach the data to it. No lorem ipsum or "Test 1".

# Environment
This shell is sandboxed: you can write only inside this directory (package-manager caches already point into ./.ui-capture/cache), and the network reaches only package registries, mise's download sources and GitHub (registry.npmjs.org, registry.yarnpkg.com, repo.yarnpkg.com, github.com, codeload.github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, nodejs.org, mise.jdx.dev, mise-versions.jdx.dev, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, binaries.prisma.sh, cdn.jsdelivr.net, unpkg.com). Docker isn't available. A process you start in the background can't be seen or stopped from a later command, so test servers on another port than 4421 (e.g. 5421) or in the foreground under `timeout`; anything still listening on 4421 is stopped before I check.

# When you're done, leave this in ./.ui-capture/
- app.json: {"mode": "static" or "server", "entry": "/path where the main UI opens", "login": null or {"username": "...", "email": "...", "password": "..."}, "stubs": [{"service": "what was faked", "how": "how"}], "notes": "how you set it up, what data is loaded, and the main areas of the app"}
- static mode: the production build in ./.ui-capture/out, with index.html as its entry. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server; unknown paths fall back to index.html.
- server mode: ./.ui-capture/start.sh, which starts everything the app needs (stubs included) in the foreground and serves the UI at http://localhost:4421/ (it gets PORT=4421). It runs with the same PATH and restrictions as your shell, plus no network at all except localhost, so everything must already be installed, built and seeded (or seeded by start.sh itself).
- Put any scripts you write for seeding or stubbing in ./.ui-capture/ too; they're kept with the setup record.

# Order of work
You have 90 minutes in total, and anything unfinished when time runs out is lost. So work in this order:
1. Get the app building and running with its stubs, and write the contract above (app.json plus out/ or start.sh), even if it has only a little data so far.
2. Then build out the data, re-running your seed and checking the app still loads after each substantial step, so that a working state with the data loaded so far is always in place.
